title: Charlton to lead push for data centres
full_text:
Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton is set to defend the data centre gold rush, pushing back against calls for a moratorium and making the economic case for going hard on attracting billions of dollars in artificial intelligence investment.
In the Australian National University Crawford School annual public policy lecture on Tuesday, Charlton - tasked by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with leading Australia's AI policy - will outline what the government wants from data centre investment and AI adoption, and its centrality to Labor's economic and innovation strategy. Charlton earlier this month brought together top universities, start-up accelerators and the CSIRO to ask what could be done to help them extract the greatest benefit from the boom.
The speech comes amid growing public unease and outright resistance to dozens of data centres popping up around the country as well as calls from the Greens and others for a moratorium on new data centres, similar to those in New York state, Texas and Singapore.
The NSW government on Monday will release a framework for the rapid growth in data centre projects around the state.
Under a three-pillar proposal by the Minns government, new data centres - from simple cloud providers that service Netflix, to large-scale AI training and inference processing facilities - will be required to fund water and energy supply to help meet the surging demand.
They will also have to be able to shed up to 25 per cent of their grid-supplied electricity for up to two hours to avoid causing price spikes during peak consumption periods. This needs to be done either through load change, such as by scheduling large tasks outside of peak periods, or by shifting to storage on site, such as batteries.
Sydney, as the largest data centre market in Australia due to its proximity to power supply and undersea cable infrastructure, already hosts 60 large-scale data centre operators including CDC, AirTrunk and NEXTDC. Another 19 large-scale data centres are currently in various stages of development.
Charlton will double down on Albanese's speech to the University of Sydney last month in which the prime minister said he wanted to make Australia a hub for AI investment, while also ensuring Australians share in the benefits and that data centres do not push up household utility prices.
